vignette: Seventy-three-year-old Thomas, a seasoned freelance journalist who once chased headlines from war zones to the front page of the New York Times, was in the middle of covering the 1984 chemical plant explosion in a small Midwestern town when the disaster unfolded. The blast ripped the tower apart in a flash of acrid orange flame that sent a wall of toxic cloud into the sky. Thomas was standing on the roof of the plant, notebook in hand, when the explosion sent him spiraling to the ground. The sudden roar, the shock of the heat on his face, and the metallic taste of blood that lingered in his mouth became the visceral markers of that night. The photos he later published-sharp, black-and-white frames of twisted steel and the charred remnants of a shattered laboratory-would carry his story for decades, but for Thomas those images would also become a silent reminder of the danger that had overtaken his life. When Thomas returned home that night, the smell of burnt coffee in the kitchen seemed to echo the scene outside. He would sit at his kitchen table, a chair bolted to the wall so the back of his seat pressed against it, and watch the room in a tense standoff. The sight of the photographs on his desktop screen would trigger the urge to reposition his body against a wall, a strategy he had begun to adopt in the weeks that followed. The very taste he associated with the explosion, the acrid sweetness of the burnt coffee that filled his mouth, would remind him of the blast's sudden onset and provoke a heightened sense of threat. In the unpredictable clamor of the city's traffic, Thomas began to feel a gnawing sense that danger could erupt again at any moment, and this unpredictability led him to avoid stepping outside in the evening, fearing an unforeseen threat. Thomas's mind would race as he listened for any creak or thud that might signal an intruder. The slightest sound-a neighbor's lawn mower, a distant siren-could set his heart racing. He found himself constantly scanning his surroundings for potential weapons, from the garden gnomes he had once thought charming to the new potted plants that seemed to conceal hidden threats. These observations amplified his perception of danger and fed a cycle in which his perception of threat fed his anxiety about not being able to handle the situation. He began to avoid any thoughts of the night he was injured, convinced that thinking about it would bring the horror back to life, a thought avoidance that left him feeling emotionally numb. The idea that he would never again feel "normal emotions" seeped into his self-talk, and he lost the sense that life could have meaning beyond the headline he had once chased. The memory of the explosion itself, a looping film that played in his mind, reinforced these patterns. Each time he recalled the sight of the twisted steel or the taste of burnt coffee, the memory felt so extreme it seemed unreal. The vividness of the event made him relive it as if it were occurring right now, forcing his body to freeze. His body would stop, the hands would tremble, and the only escape he found was to stand with his back against a wall-his only anchor against the overwhelming tide of memories. The memory also made him think he would never be able to feel normal emotions again, a belief that strengthened his negative appraisal of his emotional state. In turn, the negative appraisal drove him to spend impulsively on the latest gadgets or books, hoping the instant rush would distract him from the persistent film of the night. His compulsive spending became a maladaptive strategy that seemed to give him temporary relief, but it also triggered the memory of the explosion, as each purchase reminded him of the financial risk he had taken on the night of the blast. The cycle tightened further: the more he tried to avoid the memory, the more it surfaced, the more he felt threatened, and the more he turned to the wall for protection. Thomas's days at the newsroom became a battleground. When a new photo of the chemical plant's wreckage appeared on the newsroom screen, he would instinctively reach for the chair nearest the wall, his body tensing. He could not relax, even in the safety of the newsroom, because he was constantly listening for sounds that might mean someone was entering his space. He would stare at the picture until the image of twisted metal and the taste of burnt coffee flooded his senses. He started to refuse to read any article about other disasters, convinced that even a passing mention would remind him of his own experience. His compulsive spending had begun to strain his finances, and his sense of meaning in life had diminished to the point where the idea of writing a feature article felt meaningless. He had begun to see the world as a potential threat, every unpredictable situation a reminder that he could be next, and he feared losing the meaning he once found in telling stories. Now, in the quiet of his kitchen, Thomas is reaching out for help. The fear that he can never again feel the normal range of emotions has taken root in his mind. He is terrified that the memories will continue to intrude and that the walls he once used for protection will never allow him to find peace. What brought him to this moment, to seek therapy, was the realization that the compulsive spending was draining his savings, that his relationships-his divorce had left a gap that he could no longer fill-had begun to fray, and that each day he spent in his apartment, staring at the wall, felt like another silent witness to the past. Thomas hopes that, through understanding, he might regain a sense of meaning and, more importantly, learn to let the film of that night fade, to allow himself to feel normal emotions again.
